title: The reduce loop in C

tests.expr: ({ float x[] = {1.0f, 2.0f, 3.0f}; float r = sum_left(x, 3); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &r, 4); u; })
({ float x[] = {-0.0f}; float r = sum_left(x, 1); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &r, 4); u; })
({ float x[] = {-0.0f, -0.0f, -0.0f}; float r = sum_left(x, 3); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &r, 4); u; })
({ float x[] = {100000000.0f, -100000000.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f}; float r = sum_left(x, 4); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &r, 4); u; })
({ float x[] = {100000000.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f, -100000000.0f}; float r = sum_left(x, 4); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &r, 4); u; })
({ float x[] = {0.1f, 0.2f, 0.3f}; float r = sum_left(x, 3); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &r, 4); u; })
({ float x[] = {7.5f}; float r = sum_left(x, 1); unsigned u; memcpy(&u, &r, 4); u; })

hints: The starter's sums are right except in one case. Try a single `-0.0f`.
`0.0f + -0.0f` is `+0.0f`. Start from the first element instead: `float acc = x[0];`.
Then loop from `i = 1`. That's exactly the loop the oracle renders: an accumulator seeded with `x[0]`, and `n - 1` iterations.
explain: Seeding the accumulator with `x[0]` keeps `-0.0` and makes the loop the spec's fold exactly, one add per remaining element in order. Starting from `0.0f` is a different fold: it only differs on negative zeros, which is exactly why bit-exact grading catches it. The tests print the result's 32 bits in hex, so `-0.0` (`80000000`) and `+0.0` (`00000000`) are told apart exactly.
